# Unclaimed

Umbrellas arrived in flocks.

After any substantial rain, the evening staff at Bellweather station brought them to the lost-property office in wire trolleys: black umbrellas, striped umbrellas, umbrellas with ducks for handles, a collapsible pink one small enough to fit in a coat pocket. Martin Venn dried them, fastened their straps, and tied a numbered label to each handle. He entered them in the ledger by date, location, and description. Then he stood them in an old fire bucket until the bucket became a bouquet of crooked stems.

Most were never claimed. This was not because umbrellas were worthless, Martin thought, but because their value changed with the weather. A person might guard one fiercely through a downpour and abandon it without regret beneath the first clear sky.

Other possessions followed more mysterious routes. There were single shoes but rarely pairs, reading glasses without cases, cases without glasses, and enough gloves to equip a small orchestra. Once, someone had left a wedding cake on Platform Three. Another time, the cleaners found a suitcase containing forty jars of honey and a ceremonial sword. Martin had catalogued both without comment. After thirty-one years, he had learned that surprise was usually a failure of imagination.

His office lay beneath the western staircase, down a corridor that smelled faintly of dust and radiator paint. A frosted window admitted light from the station wall but no view. On winter afternoons, Martin switched on the green desk lamp at half past three. He liked the pool of light it made, the neat boundaries of it. Beyond the lamp lay shelves, boxes, and the unclaimed evidence of thousands of interrupted journeys.

In January, a notice appeared on the office door.

**CENTRALISATION of LOST PROPERTY SERVICES**, it announced. From the first of April, belongings would be transported to a depot outside the city, photographed, and entered into a database. Passengers could make enquiries online. The notice used the phrase *improved customer experience* twice.

Martin read it while holding his morning tea. Then he went inside, put the tea on a coaster, and continued sorting a box of scarves.

His retirement had already been arranged for the end of March. He had not connected the two events until that morning, though everyone else seemed to have done so. The station manager stopped by to say it was tidy timing. The woman from personnel used the word *natural*. Martin nodded. He had reached an age at which other people considered his endings natural.

He was sixty-three, a widower only in the sense that his ex-wife had married someone else, which was not the sense at all. Their marriage had ended twenty years earlier, without cruelty and without much conversation. Since then he had lived in a two-room flat above a shuttered tobacconist’s. He cooked on a small stove, read history books with cracked spines, and took his holidays in May, when the galleries were quiet.

His sister Nora sent him a postcard every Christmas. She lived near the Northumberland coast with her husband, a variable number of dogs, and a garden that appeared to be losing some long argument with the wind. Each postcard contained an invitation. Come for Easter. Come in summer. Come before we’re too old to be interesting. The most recent said only: *Spare room still here. Needs painting. So do you.*

Martin had put it in his locker, beneath a clean shirt.

On the first Thursday of every month, at approximately ten past ten, Violet March came to ask about a handbag.

She had done so for nearly twelve years. Martin knew the description by heart: dark green leather, short strap, brass clasp, a scuff on the base shaped like a comma. It had disappeared somewhere between the ticket hall and the 4:18 train to Marlow on the seventeenth of March. Inside were two keys, a library card, a paperback novel, an expired prescription, and a white envelope containing a note.

The first time, Mrs March had filled in the proper form. On subsequent visits, Martin simply wrote the date on the back of her enquiry card and added: *No match.*

“I don’t suppose it will have turned up,” she usually said.

“It’s unlikely now.”

“Yes. Well.”

She never seemed offended by his honesty. She was small and straight-backed, with silver hair pinned firmly at the sides. In winter she wore a grey coat with a velvet collar; in summer, a blue linen jacket. She always declined a chair. Sometimes she asked whether anyone had handed in a particular umbrella, though she had not lost one, or remarked on the state of the trains. These conversations gave her visits the appearance of ordinary errands.

Once, early on, Martin had asked whether the handbag itself was valuable.

“Not to anyone sensible,” she said.

He had waited, but she offered nothing further, and he had been trained not to press people. Lost-property work required an unusual combination of curiosity and restraint. You could examine a thing closely enough to describe its stitching while knowing almost nothing about the person who missed it.

In February, with six weeks remaining, Martin began clearing the upper shelves. The database people had sent instructions about photographing items, but there seemed little point in photographing twelve-year-old gloves destined for charity or disposal. He worked from left to right, wearing cotton gloves when handling jewellery and an old pair of gardening gloves for everything else.

Behind a box marked **WINTER ACCESSORIES 2009**, he found a canvas holdall swollen with damp. A leaking pipe had stained one side. Inside were a child’s red mitten, three paperbacks fused at the corners, a set of keys, and a green handbag.

He saw the brass clasp first.

Martin took the handbag to his desk. He did not feel excitement exactly. His response was more physical: a slight lift behind the ribs, followed by the need to sit down.

The leather had darkened where water touched it, but the scuff on the base was unmistakable. A faded label hung from the strap. Someone had written **brown holdall and contents**, then added a location code for a platform at the opposite end of the station. The handbag had been swept into a larger loss and disappeared inside its description.

He unfastened the clasp.

Two keys lay in the inner pocket. The library card had softened with age. The paperback was a murder mystery with a train on its cover. In a side compartment Martin found a folded prescription and, beneath it, a white envelope. The paper had yellowed, but the envelope was unsealed. A single initial, **V**, appeared on the front in faded blue ink.

He closed the bag without opening it.

For the rest of the day, he moved between satisfaction and an obscure sense of injury. The bag had been thirty feet from Mrs March every time she visited. It had waited through her grey coats and blue jackets, through changes in stationery and three separate revisions of the enquiry form. He imagined explaining this to her. He also imagined not explaining it, which would be simpler and somehow worse.

The first Thursday in March was eight days away.

Martin waited until ten past ten. At twenty past, he told himself that her train might be delayed. At eleven, he went upstairs and bought a cup of coffee he did not want. When he returned, a young man was at the counter asking whether anyone had handed in a black hat.

By half past twelve, Martin had checked the office doorway so often that the temporary assistant noticed.

“Expecting someone?” she asked.

“No,” he said.

Mrs March did not come that day, or the next. On Saturday morning, Martin took her original enquiry card from the index drawer. There was a telephone number, but the line had been disconnected. The address was on the other side of the city, not far from the river.

He told himself that lost-property staff did not make personal deliveries. Then he put the handbag in a clean carrier bag and caught the bus.

The journey took fifty minutes. Martin sat near the front with the bag upright between his knees. Outside, the city passed in pieces: a row of barbershops, a church converted into apartments, men pressure-washing the steps of a closed cinema. At a traffic light, a girl in a school uniform waved at someone on the pavement, then looked embarrassed by the size of her own enthusiasm.

Martin had rarely travelled this way on a Saturday. He knew the station intimately and the city around it in fragments. It occurred to him that most of his knowledge of other people’s lives had arrived without faces. A violin suggested music, but not ambition. A suitcase suggested departure, though it might just as easily mean return. Even grief could be mistaken for carelessness when reduced to an object on a shelf.

Mrs March’s address belonged to a narrow brick building with four doorbells. A woman in her forties opened the main door before Martin could press one. She held a rubbish bag in one hand and regarded him with the alert weariness of someone expecting bad news.

When he introduced himself, her expression changed.

“The station?” she said. “You’d better come up.”

She was Mrs March’s daughter, Caroline. Her mother had fallen in December and broken her hip. She was recovering well, but stairs and buses had become negotiations. Caroline had been staying three nights a week.

“She didn’t tell you?” Martin asked.

“Tell you? She barely told me.” Caroline looked at the carrier bag. “Is that what I think it is?”

“Oh,” she said.

Martin set it on the table. He had prepared an explanation involving water damage, an incorrect label, and the limitations of the old shelving system. None of it seemed useful.

“We found it,” he said.

Mrs March unfastened the brass clasp. Her hands were swollen at the knuckles, and Caroline moved to help, but her mother shook her head. She removed the library card, the keys, and the ruined paperback. When she reached the envelope, she stopped.

“Would you like some tea, Mr Venn?” she asked.

“Only if you were making some.”

“I wasn’t. Caroline will.”

Caroline gave a small snort and filled the kettle.

“It isn’t a love letter,” Mrs March said at last. “You look as though you’re bracing yourself.”

Martin turned back. She was smiling, though her eyes had reddened.

“Arthur wrote it during our first week of marriage. We had a disagreement about shopping. I can’t remember the disagreement, only that I went out in a state of tremendous principle and came back with potatoes.”

She handed him the paper. In narrow blue handwriting, it said:

*V—

“He had already bought potatoes,” she said. “That was his idea of an apology. Mine was cooking them.”

She folded the note along its original crease.

“Later, I used it as a bookmark. Then I kept moving it from book to book because I didn’t want to lose it.”
